The Later Han: The Liu family ruled with their capital at Luoyang.
It was in the third year of Yongping, the year of Gengshen,
that Emperor Xiaoming dreamed of a golden man with the light of the sun and moon upon his neck flying into the palace courtyard.
The Emperor questioned his ministers.
The Grand Historian Fu Yi replied,
"Your servant has heard that in the Western Regions there is a deity called Buddha.
Is it not he whom Your Majesty dreamed of?"
In the seventh year, during the cyclical year of Jiazi,

the Emperor issued an edict for Langzhong Cai Yin, Zhonglangjiang Qin Jing, and Boshi Wang Zun, along with seventeen others— eighteen people in total— to travel westward in search of the Buddha-dharma.
Kāṅ and his companions reached the kingdom of India and invited Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna to return with them;
they used white horses to carry the scriptures and brought back painted images of Śākyamuni Buddha.
In the tenth year of Yongping, the year being Dingmao, he arrived at Luoyang.
The Emperor was delighted and established the Baima Monastery.
This continued until the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year, the year being Xinwei.
The Daoist masters of the Five Peaks, including Chu Shixin and others, harbored resentment and were displeased.
During the formal audience for the New Year, they submitted a memorial requesting a formal contest.
By imperial decree, Song Xiang, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was dispatched to usher them into the Changle Palace.
The Emperor said, "On the fifteenth day of this month, there shall be a great assembly at the southern gate of the Baima Monastery.
On that day, you and your followers shall place the various scriptures of the *Lingbao* upon an altar to the east of the Way."
The Emperor placed the scriptures, images, and śarīra relics upon a pavilion of seven treasures to the west of the Way;
Xìn and the others circumambulated the altar, weeping and prostrating themselves as they earnestly entreated the Celestial Honored One with sincere and fervent words.
Furthermore, they burned the scriptures with sandalwood fuel and other materials,
hoping that the scriptures would remain undamaged as a sign of their divine wonder;
however, the scriptures being burned were all reduced to ashes.
Previously, he had been able to ascend to heaven, enter fire, tread upon water, and make himself invisible, but now he could no longer do so.
When those skilled in incantations called upon him or urged him forward, he did not respond.
At that time, the Grand Tutor Zhang Yan said to Xun:
Since the trials yielded no results, they were proven to be false and deceptive;
it was therefore appropriate to seek the true Dharma of the Western Regions.
At that time, the Daoist Fei Shucaí and others of Mount Nanyue died in a state of shame and self-reproach.
At that time, the light from the Buddha’s relics was five-colored;
it rose straight up into the air, swirling like a canopy,
covering the entire assembly and eclipsing the sun.
The Dharma Master Mātanga was previously an Arhat;
he could travel through the air by means of his supernormal powers, sitting and reclining with sovereign mastery over spiritual transformations.
At that time, celestial jewel-flowers rained down and various musical instruments were played.
They moved the hearts of the people, and the great assembly rejoiced.
Kāśyapa Mātanga sat down again, and Dharmaratna preached the Dharma;
at that time, the multitude were all filled with joy, having experienced something unprecedented.
At that time, one hundred and ninety women from the inner palace, including Lady Yin and Consort Wang, entered the monastic life; as did Liu Shanjun,
Marquis of Yangcheng and Minister of Works, and Jiang Gouer, General Who Guards the Far Reaches.
Two hundred and sixty-eight people left the household life as monastics. Six hundred and twenty people,
including the Daoist masters of the Four Peaks, Lü Huītōng and others,
also left the household life as monastics.
Three hundred and ninety-one men and women from Zhangzi, Shang'e, Pan, and other regions in the capital region entered the monastic order;
the Emperor personally shaved the heads of those who had become renunciants along with his various officials.
He provided offerings and sustenance for thirty days and constructed ten monasteries:
seven outside the city walls and three within the city.
Seven temples were established for monks and three temples for nuns,
as fully recounted in the transmission within the *Fǎběn nèi zhuàn* (Inner Record of the Dharma) of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
[There was] the śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga.
A native of Central India of Brahmin descent;
from his youth he was quick-witted and possessed of refined elegance.

He was widely learned and possessed vast erudition, being exceptionally clear-sighted regarding the sutras and vinaya; his power of reflection was precise and profound, as he explored the subtle and probed the deep.
He expounded the texts and analyzed their hidden meanings, and every time a new interpretation emerged, it seemed to transcend the realm of the mundane.
Once, while traveling through a small kingdom in Western India,
he was invited to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
Shortly thereafter, a neighboring country raised an army and marched against it.
Just as he was about to enter the territory, he was obstructed by circumstances such that his troops could not advance.
The soldiers of that country suspected he possessed some supernatural artifice and secretly dispatched an envoy to spy on him.
They saw only the ruler and his ministers sitting at ease together, listening to his exposition of the Mahāyāna sūtras concerning the methods for protecting the state through the Earth-Deva Kings.
Thereupon, having witnessed these divine manifestations, that kingdom requested peace and sought the Dharma.
At that time, Cai Yin and others earnestly entreated Dharmaratna,
who subsequently came together with Yin and the others.
He saw the Emperor in Luoyang;
in the tenth year of Yongping, the year being Dingmao,
he translated [the text] at Baima Temple.
The Sutra in Forty-two Sections, one fascicle.
This sutra was originally an excerpt from foreign scriptures.
An Shigao [Dharmaratna] transcribed it because, at the beginning of the Great Transformation, people had not yet attained deep faith.
He retained his profound understanding without translating many works;
instead, he extracted the essential points of the sutras to guide the common people of the age.
He passed away in Luoyang during the Later Qin dynasty.
The śramaṇa Dharmaratna was a native of Central India. From his youth,
he possessed keen insight and profound refinement, and was widely learned and deeply compassionate.
He was extensively proficient in meditative contemplation and the Vinaya, exhausting their subtle depths.
He recited over one million words of scripture and had more than a thousand disciples.
In his dwelling, he sought not comfort, always harboring the intent to bring vast benefit.
His observance of the precepts was so rigorous that none could peer into its depths.
When he encountered [Dharmakṣema] seeking his request, he immediately conceived the ambition to travel light; however, the ruler of the state would not permit it.
Mili arrived later than An Shigao, traveling by circuitous routes.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, he initially translated the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* together with An Shigao.
After An Shigao passed away, Mili arrived in the year Wuchen (the 11th year of Yongping) and remained until the year Gengwu (the 13th year).

Initially, Emperor Wu dredged the Kunming Pond and obtained ash and ink.
He questioned Dongfang Shuo,

When Dharmaratna arrived at that time, he was questioned about it;

Furthermore, he brought a sandalwood image of King Udayana to Luoyang;

His conduct was pure and profound, and his nature was open and quick-witted.
He observed the precepts of the Dharma and recited the various sutras.
His resolve was to propagate the teachings and travel abroad to transform sentient beings.

The śramaṇa Anqing, style name Shigao,
was the crown prince of the kingdom of Parthia.
When his father the king passed away, he yielded the throne to his uncle and left the household life to travel abroad.
From the second year of the Jianhe era of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty until his passing,
not long passed before he became highly proficient in the Chinese language.
Initially, he claimed that he had been a monastic in a previous life.
There was a fellow student who was prone to anger.
Gao said to him, "Because of this, you shall receive an evil form; I will certainly deliver you."
He then took his leave, saying,
"I am going to Guangzhou to settle an old karmic debt.
Upon arriving in Panyu, he encountered a youth on the road who drew a sword and pointed it at him.
Laughing loudly, he said,
"I have come specifically to repay you.
He then extended his neck to receive the blade.
Thereupon, he restored his body to its original tall form and continued translating the scriptures as before.
After a long time, he said:
He intended to save his former classmate from the past;
thus he traveled on until he reached the temple by Lake Quting.
The deity of the temple was stern and fierce, so the boatmen offered prayers to the shrine.
The incantation-master called out to Gao, saying:
"In the past, we studied together; now your life has reached its end, and it is but a matter of days.
I fear that this hideous form will defile the rivers and lakes."
I am currently in the West Marsh of Mount Si and fear falling into hell.
Now, having a thousand bolts of silk and various treasures, I pray that you will build a stupa for me.
Fearing that the multitude would be terrified if he manifested his hideous form,
Gao said, "Just manifest it;
there is no cause for distress."
The deity then emerged with its head revealed; it was a great python.
Gao directed his foreign speech toward it, chanting it as hymns of praise.
The python withdrew in tears of sorrow.
When Taida arrived in Yuzhang, Gao immediately built a temple for him.
At the very beginning of the construction, there was a young man;
after Gao had finished bestowing the ritual prayers upon him, the youth suddenly vanished.
Gao said, "He has attained liberation from his evil form. Later,
people saw a dead python in a marsh in the mountains west of Shan, its head and tail spanning several li.

The Snake Village in Xunyang Commandery today is that very place. Daogao again traveled to Guangzhou to seek out the youth who had previously harmed him; he was still there. Together they spoke of their past karmic connection, saying: [...text omitted... Daogao said: "I am now seventy years old. My life is at its end and my strength is exhausted. I have no desire to remain in this world for long. I wish to go to Mount Lu to see the Master of the Dharma (Huiyuan). I hope you will not begrudge me your company. The youth replied: "I have heard that the Master of the Dharma is a man of great virtue and wisdom. I have long desired to pay him homage. I shall accompany you with joy. They traveled together to Mount Lu. When they arrived at the mountain gate, they encountered the monk Sengfu, who asked them: "Where are you two going? Daogao replied: "We are going to see the Master of the Dharma. Sengfu said: "The Master of the Dharma has already passed away. He died on the eighth day of the second month of this year. Upon hearing this, Daogao wept uncontrollably. The youth comforted him, saying: "The Master of the Dharma is a person of great spiritual power. His passing must have been due to some profound cause. You should not grieve so excessively. Daogao said: "I have lived in the world for over seventy years. I have never seen such a calamity as this. How could I not mourn? The youth said: "Do not speak of it like this. The Master of the Dharma has attained the Way. His passing is not something to be lamented. Furthermore, you should consider that the Master of the Dharma is currently residing in the Pure Land. You should instead rejoice and offer prayers for his rebirth. Daogao then composed a poem to express his grief: *My heart is heavy and my body weak;* *My spirit is weary and my strength spent.* *In the vast expanse of the world,* *I have wandered through the four directions.* *Now I encounter this great sorrow;* *How can I bear to live another day?* Having finished the poem, he wept even more bitterly. The youth took him by the hand and led him back to the monastery. There, they saw the Master of the Dharma’s remains lying in state. Daogao prostrated himself before the coffin and wailed: "I have come from afar to see you, yet you have already departed. What can I do? The youth said: "The Master of the Dharma has already been cremated. His relics are enshrined in a stupa. You may go there to pay your respects. Daogao went to the stupa and offered incense. He then circumambulated it three times and departed. As he walked away, he looked back one last time and wept. The youth said: "You have already seen the Master of the Dharma. Why do you still weep? Daogao replied: "I have seen his physical form, but I have not yet seen his true nature. I hope that in the future we may meet again in the Pure Land. The youth said: "The Master of the Dharma has already been reborn in the Pure Land. We shall surely meet there. Daogao and the youth then parted ways. Daogao returned to Mount Lu, while the youth remained there. Later, when Daogao was about to pass away, he called the youth to his side and said: "I have lived a full life. My time has come. I shall soon depart. The youth asked: "Where will you be reborn? Daogao replied: "I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. The youth asked: "When will you arrive? Daogao replied: "In seven days. On the seventh day, Daogao passed away peacefully. The youth performed the funeral rites according to the Dharma. He then returned to Guangzhou. This concludes the account of Daogao and the youth. It is recorded that Daogao was a man of great virtue and learning, well-versed in both Buddhist and secular classics. His reputation for integrity and wisdom spread far and wide. The youth, too, was a man of noble character and deep faith. Their meeting and subsequent parting are truly a remarkable tale of karmic connection. Thus ends the record.

The Prince’s character and conduct were such that he sought to transform others;
